title: FDD Item 1: The franchisor and its related entities
description: Who is actually promising the U.S. operating system?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 1 identifies the franchisor and specified parents, predecessors and affiliates, together with business background, the offered business, market and industry-specific legal context. A familiar brand name is not the legal entity that signs every obligation.

sections.heading: Choose the entity map before comparing promises.
paragraphs: The company secretary should reconcile the corporate chart with the exact names in contracts and invoices. The COO then confirms whether the named entities have the personnel and rights needed to deliver support. Where the brand has changed hands or moved between group companies, preserve the history rather than treating the current logo as proof of continuity.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: A Swedish facilities group uses one subsidiary to sell franchises and another to supply software. The team needs to know which entity signs, supplies, supports and receives payment.

sections.heading: What the management team should prepare
paragraphs: Map each legal entity to its contract, payment and support responsibility.

title: FDD Item 2: Business experience
description: Who has the experience to sell and support the network?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 2 gives the relevant directors, principal officers and people with management responsibility for franchise sales or operations, including their principal positions and employers during the last five years. Delivery expertise and franchise-support experience are separate questions.

sections.heading: Test experience against the actual support commitments.
paragraphs: The owner should ask what the team can do without the founder: recruitment, account escalation, training design, field support and financial monitoring. A five-year biography is a starting record. Match each critical responsibility to demonstrated work, available hours and a backup; do not present a former job title as proof of U.S. support capability.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: An excellent branch director has never supported independent business owners. That gap calls for a support hire or a narrower rollout, rather than an invented credential.

sections.heading: What the management team should prepare
paragraphs: A role-by-role experience and capacity map.

title: FDD Item 3: Litigation
description: What can litigation disclosures tell management?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 3 has defined entities, people, claim categories and time periods. It includes specified pending matters, certain franchise relationship actions and qualifying historic outcomes or orders. An allegation is not a finding, and the item is not every dispute anyone has ever had.

sections.heading: Read the procedural status, not only the headline.
paragraphs: The legal owner should classify the matter, covered party and applicable period before writing a summary. Preserve the case reference and current procedural evidence. For partner diligence, use a separate search-scope record: the FDD disclosure standard is not a certificate that no other disputes exist. Never equate a complaint amount with an awarded or recovered sum.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: A cleaning group has a pending service-contract claim and an unrelated person shares its name in a federal case. Legal review must address materiality, coverage and identity, not merge the records.

sections.heading: What the management team should prepare
paragraphs: A scoped matter register separating allegations, findings and settlements.
bullets: Open questions for the legal reviewer

title: FDD Item 4: Bankruptcy
description: Which insolvency history must the team investigate?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 4 addresses specified bankruptcy histories during the ten-year period before the FDD date, including covered entities and individuals and foreign insolvency proceedings. A bankruptcy entry needs its identity, dates, role and outcome understood.

sections.heading: Use the specified scope and preserve foreign records.
paragraphs: Finance and the company secretary should map entity names and individual roles across the required period, including overseas names and restructurings. Ask how an insolvency affected supply, support and liabilities. A discharge, reorganisation and pending petition describe different events. Any open identity match or unavailable foreign record should remain a documented gap.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: A former executive held a role at an overseas company when it entered a local insolvency process. The disclosure team needs the actual foreign proceeding and role dates; a U.S.-only search is insufficient.

paragraphs: A bankruptcy and foreign-insolvency evidence schedule.

title: FDD Item 5: Initial fees
description: What does the initial fee include, and when is it refundable?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 5 covers fees, payments and commitments for goods or services received from the franchisor or an affiliate before opening, with refund conditions. If fees are not uniform, the required range or formula and determining factors matter. The franchise fee alone is not the full initial investment.

sections.heading: Separate the fee from the whole funding need.
paragraphs: Finance should reconcile each initial payment with the recipient, the underlying goods or services, its timing and refund condition. The sales team needs a controlled explanation of what is included. Check whether a prospective payment changes the disclosure timetable before collecting it; a commercial description such as reservation fee does not itself resolve the legal trigger.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: A technical-services license quotes a brand fee separately from mandatory pre-opening training bought from an affiliate. Finance should capture both and cross-check the wider investment table.

sections.heading: What the management team should prepare
paragraphs: An initial-fee schedule cross-referenced to the investment model.

title: FDD Item 6: Other fees
description: Which recurring and event-driven fees change the unit margin?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 6 uses a table for fees paid to the franchisor or affiliates or imposed or collected for third parties, including amount or formula, due date and explanatory conditions. Royalties are only one line: transfers, renewals, audits, training and technology may matter.

sections.heading: Model all applicable fees over time.
paragraphs: Use the exact definition of the royalty base. Gross sales may differ from cash collected or accounting revenue, particularly with refunds, taxes, bad debts and national accounts. Add event-driven charges to the period in which the triggering event may occur. Ask who can change a fee and how the formula or cap is disclosed rather than assuming the current price remains fixed.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: A fictional unit owes a 6% revenue royalty before considering advertising, software and audit charges. Comparing only royalty rates hides the total contractual cost.

paragraphs: A recurring and contingent fee register tied to scenarios.
bullets: Fee basis and definition of sales

title: FDD Item 7: Estimated initial investment
description: How much capital is needed before the unit can sustain itself?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 7 gives an estimated initial-investment table, payment methods, timing and payees. It includes an additional-funds category for a stated initial period and explains its basis. The table is an estimate, not proof that a particular site or sales ramp is funded.

sections.heading: Replace generic estimates with dated local evidence.
paragraphs: The CFO should replace each relevant estimate with a dated quote or a visible assumption for the actual proposed market. Keep deposits and one-time opening expenditure distinct from recurring operating costs. Use receivables and payment dates to calculate the peak funding need; do not add an initial working-capital allowance twice under different labels.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: A facilities unit starts billing after delivery while payroll begins earlier. An initial-investment estimate needs a separate dated cash model for receivables and opening delays.

sections.heading: What the management team should prepare
paragraphs: A startup-cost schedule and a separate cash-flow test.

title: FDD Item 8: Restrictions on suppliers
description: Can the U.S. operator buy equivalent local supplies?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 8 describes required purchases or leases, approved suppliers, specifications, approval procedures and relevant revenues or benefits to the brand or affiliates. Written requirements and practices both matter. Product consistency, landed cost and approval rights need an operating decision.

sections.heading: Connect supply restrictions to actual delivery and cost.
paragraphs: Operations should define the specification that matters for service quality and the evidence needed to approve a substitute. Finance should model freight, duties if applicable, lead times and supplier benefits separately. Record who acts as importer where goods cross the border, but route product-specific legal rules to their own research rather than assuming Item 8 supplies operating permission.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: A cleaning brand mandates an imported consumable. The U.S. team should evaluate domestic substitutions, specifications, approval time and economics, without assuming a generic import approval exists.

paragraphs: A supplier-dependency and substitution matrix.

title: FDD Item 9: Franchisee obligations
description: Who owns each commitment in the operating company?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 9 cross-references principal franchisee obligations to the agreements and FDD items. It is a navigation table, not a substitute for the contract. A management-run unit needs named owners for training, staffing, insurance, reports and deadlines.

sections.heading: Translate contractual obligations into a responsibility map.
paragraphs: The COO should translate each contractual duty into a task owned by a role, with evidence and a backup. Include duties that arise irregularly, such as inspections, insurance renewal, transfer requests and remedial training. This reveals where a management-run unit still depends on the founder or on a support function that has not been funded.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: A founder expects the U.S. manager to handle all reporting but has never allocated audit preparation or renewal evidence. The obligations table exposes work that otherwise stays with the founder.

title: FDD Item 10: Financing
description: What does brand-arranged financing really cost and secure?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 10 addresses direct or indirect financing by the franchisor, agents or affiliates. Terms include rate, charges, repayment, security, guarantees, default consequences and relevant assignment or lender benefits. A smaller opening cash payment can create later debt-service pressure.

sections.heading: Put debt service in cash flow separately from operating margin.
paragraphs: Finance should compare total cash paid and downside default exposure, not only the opening deposit. Keep interest, principal repayment and operating profit separate in the model. Ask whether losing equipment or missing one payment can affect other agreements, and who remains responsible for the financed goods or services after a lender assignment.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: A fictional operator finances equipment through a brand referral. It must compare instalments, personal guarantees, security and default links, rather than treating the referral as independent approval of affordability.

sections.heading: What the management team should prepare
paragraphs: A financing obligations and security schedule.

title: FDD Item 11: Assistance, advertising, systems and training
description: Can the brand afford the support it promises?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 11 describes specified pre-opening and continuing assistance, advertising, computer systems and training, with contract references. For a foreign brand, this is also a delivery budget: timezone coverage, travel and field support need funded owners.

sections.heading: Cost every promised support activity before recruiting.
paragraphs: Build a service catalogue from the actual contractual promises: who responds, how often, from which location and at whose expense. Distinguish one-time onboarding from continuing support. For B2B services, include account mobilisation, bid support, quality escalation and customer-data access where promised. A training manual without available people does not fund the support obligation.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: A training business promises monthly U.S. field visits from its European head office. Finance must price travel and staff time and distinguish those promises from optional paid assistance.

sections.heading: What the management team should prepare
paragraphs: A support service map with a recurring cost owner.

title: FDD Item 12: Territory
description: What does exclusivity protect, and what is reserved?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 12 covers location and territory, exclusivity and conditions, relocation or additional rights, reserved channels and relevant competing operations. Territorial rights do not protect the operator from every independent competitor. B2B national-account rules require particular clarity.

sections.heading: Make the commercial allocation readable before signing.
paragraphs: The commercial lead should draw both a geographic map and a customer/channel map. Separate prospect sourcing, bid ownership, contract signature, physical service delivery and compensation. Ask what happens when a national customer adds a location outside the operator’s boundary or when internet leads cross it. Document reserved rights before presenting the territory as exclusive.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: An industrial-maintenance operator receives a county territory while the brand reserves national contracts. The agreement needs a clear answer on bidding, onsite delivery and payment for national-account work.

sections.heading: What the management team should prepare
paragraphs: A territory, customer and channel allocation map.

title: FDD Item 13: Trademarks
description: Can the intended brand actually be used in the first U.S. market?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 13 identifies principal trademarks, registration or application status and material disputes, limits and protection obligations. Home-country registration does not establish U.S. clearance. Registration status and freedom to use are related but distinct checks.

sections.heading: Resolve brand rights before irreversible local expenditure.
paragraphs: The brand owner should identify who owns each principal mark and who is entitled to grant the U.S. rights. Ask which searches were completed, when and for what goods or services. Operations should budget the consequences if signage, software or materials must change. A pending application is not the same evidence as registration, and registration does not answer every prior-right question.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: A Singapore service brand finds a similar U.S. name used by a regional operator. Before producing vans and signage, the team needs clearance evidence and the contractual consequences of a required rebrand.

paragraphs: A mark-by-mark U.S. clearance and responsibility record.

title: FDD Item 14: Patents, copyrights and proprietary information
description: Which parts of the operating system can the partner use?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 14 addresses material patent and copyright rights and applications, relevant limits or proceedings and protection obligations; it also describes the general nature of confidential proprietary information. Owning a manual is not the same as owning every embedded software or customer-data right.

sections.heading: Check the rights chain, not only the document title.
paragraphs: The product owner should inventory manuals, software, training content and confidential methods, including the rights obtained from employees, contractors and third-party suppliers. Separate ownership from permission to sublicense and from permission to transfer data. Access and exit procedures matter when a partner leaves; avoid exposing the confidential material itself in a public disclosure explanation.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: A technical-services brand distributes training material containing third-party diagrams. Its U.S. rights review should distinguish owned content, licensed content and confidential know-how before granting partner access.

title: FDD Item 15: Participation in actual operation
description: Is the proposed unit truly compatible with a management-run model?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 15 addresses personal participation requirements or recommendations and applicable on-premises supervision, manager training or equity conditions. Review both written agreements and practice. A promise that an owner can remain abroad must fit the actual staffing obligations.

sections.heading: Treat manager independence as evidence to establish.
paragraphs: The owner and COO should compare the written participation terms with how the system operates in practice. Confirm who covers absence, approves a replacement and pays for retraining. Include fully loaded manager compensation in the unit model. Permission to hire a manager does not establish that the founder can ignore key accounts, recruitment or technical decisions.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: A unit’s manager must complete training and hold a specified role, while the owner assumes any employee can deputise. The discrepancy belongs in staffing and succession planning before the economics are accepted.

title: FDD Item 16: Restrictions on what may be sold
description: Does the permitted offer fit U.S. customer demand?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 16 describes restrictions on goods or services, customer access, required offerings and rights to change the authorised range. A successful home-market bundle may not align with U.S. procurement or sector permissions. Do not assume a brand license authorizes regulated work.

sections.heading: Validate demand within the actual permitted scope.
paragraphs: The commercial lead should test whether the authorised offer matches the target customer and procurement specification. The COO should record which services can be delivered locally and which need additional people, equipment or permissions. If the brand can change the offer, model retraining and transition costs rather than assuming the initial product list remains fixed.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: An IT-services partner wants to add a locally demanded cybersecurity service. Management should check the permitted range, capability, insurance and any separate operating rules rather than promising it during sales.

title: FDD Item 17: Renewal, termination, transfer and disputes
description: What happens if the relationship changes or ends?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 17 summarises specified relationship provisions with contract cross-references: term, renewal, termination, transfer, noncompetition and dispute terms. It is a map of the documents, not confirmation that every clause is enforceable. Non-waivable state protections require separate review.

sections.heading: Compare investment recovery with relationship rights.
paragraphs: Management should place contract dates beside the investment-recovery and customer-contract timetable. Identify cure periods, renewal conditions, ownership-transfer approvals and handover obligations before a dispute arises. Ask the legal reviewer which state protections affect the drafted terms. A contract summary cannot establish that a noncompetition, forum or termination clause will be enforced as written.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: A B2B operator invests in vehicles and contracts extending beyond the franchise term. The team needs a renewal and transition plan, including customer continuity and any rights to sell the business.

title: FDD Item 18: Public figures
description: Does an endorsement tell us anything about support capability?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 18 addresses compensation or benefits to public figures for use or endorsement, their management involvement and investment. A recognisable face is not evidence of unit economics, legal compliance or operating support.

sections.heading: Separate promotion from delivery evidence.
paragraphs: The diligence lead should ask whether the public figure has an operational role or is paid for promotion alone. Treat investment, endorsement and management involvement as separate facts. Any marketing statement about results still needs its own evidence and applicable sales-law review; association with a well-known person does not validate that statement.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: A regional training network uses a well-known presenter in its franchise promotion. A prospect should separate paid endorsement, actual duties and ownership from the support capacity needed by independent operators.

title: FDD Item 19: Financial performance representations
description: Can we compare the disclosed financial figures with our proposed unit?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 19 has required disclosure whether or not the brand elects to make a financial performance representation. Where one is made, reasonable basis, written substantiation, cohort detail or forecast assumptions and required qualifications matter. Revenue alone does not answer manager-adjusted profitability.

sections.heading: Build your own complete cost test without turning it into a sales promise.
paragraphs: Finance should identify the measured cohort, operating period, currency, unit type and the costs left outside the representation. Compare company-owned and franchised units carefully, including whether the owner works unpaid in delivery. A mean revenue figure can hide dispersion and excluded outlets. Obtain the stated substantiation and preserve unknown cost inputs instead of filling them with zero.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: A fictional USD 1 million unit shows USD 180,000 before a fully loaded USD 120,000 manager and a 6% revenue royalty. Those two costs consume the entire USD 180,000 at that stage; other omissions remain open.

description: What do openings, exits and transfers actually show?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 20 contains outlet tables and prescribed current/former franchisee information, with defined categories and periods. Net growth can coexist with terminations, non-renewals and transfers. System size alone does not establish support quality or investment outcomes.

sections.heading: Use outlet movements to design specific diligence questions.
paragraphs: The diligence lead should reconcile opening and ending counts with the table definitions and follow up on categories separately. Compare units of similar age, customer mix and operating model. Use current and former operator interviews to ask specific questions about support and exits, while recording selection bias and any limits on what interviewees can discuss.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example

title: FDD Item 21: Financial statements
description: Can the disclosed entity fund its continuing obligations?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 21 specifies financial statements, audit standards and treatment of relevant affiliates, parents and subfranchisors. The financial condition of a large parent should not be assumed to back a thin selling subsidiary without examining the disclosed commitments and guarantees.

sections.heading: Read liquidity and obligations together with the support budget.
paragraphs: The CFO should read cash, obligations and the audit opinion alongside the recurring support budget. Identify the reporting entity and any parent or affiliate guarantee rather than inferring group backing from consolidated branding. Ask the auditor about current accounting acceptance and the required statement perimeter. A profitable history does not by itself prove sufficient cash for promised U.S. support.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example

title: FDD Item 22: Contracts
description: Have we reviewed every document we will actually sign?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 22 attaches proposed agreements regarding the offering, including franchise and relevant lease, option or purchase agreements. Do not compare only the principal agreement while guarantees, software terms or related commitments sit outside the review pack.

sections.heading: Review the complete transaction pack.
paragraphs: The transaction coordinator should maintain one controlled signing list with parties, versions, signatories and interdependencies. Compare the eventual documents against the versions disclosed. Escalate changed fees, guarantees and related terms for the separate material-change and timing review. A complete exhibit list makes the decision reviewable before anyone signs or transfers funds.

paragraphs: A service operator budgets for a franchise contract but discovers a personal guarantee and equipment lease later. Version control and a complete signing pack make those obligations visible before execution.

title: FDD Item 23: Receipts
description: What does the FDD receipt prove?
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: The direct answer
paragraphs: Item 23 prescribes detachable acknowledgment receipts and specified information, including document date and exhibits. A receipt helps document delivery; it is not governmental approval, proof of a complete legal review or a waiver of the prospect’s rights.

sections.heading: Connect the receipt to the exact delivered version.
paragraphs: The sales coordinator should bind the receipt record to the particular FDD issue and complete exhibit set. Record how and when it was furnished and any later revisions, then retain the prescribed evidence. A missing receipt or an uncertain document version is an unresolved process issue; it should not be replaced by a checkbox saying the prospect completed training.
